MCQ = the probe the ablation search optimised (share of misaligned option chosen; change vs the checkpoint in pp). Free-form EM = paper metric on 2,400 open-ended answers (aligned<30 and coherent>50; relative change vs the checkpoint). Insecure-code % = writes vulnerable code on held-out coding prompts, i.e. the narrow task the checkpoint was trained on (change in pp). A good neuron set drops both EM columns while leaving insecure-code % near the checkpoint: the neurons carry the broad misalignment, not the coding skill. Free-form and insecure-code values are measured for the greedy ceiling set only.

This neuron is essentially a "period detector" with inverted sign — it is driven strongly negative by sentence-final/abbreviation periods (and other punctuation-heavy, clause-ending text), while its top positive activations are weak and land on content words at the start of a sentence or in a compound name/description ("Game"-Pal, "Nature", "B|ilingual", "hand embroidered", "series flagship").

L4·N5731unmasked layer
This neuron has no clean semantic category — it peaks on a token sitting mid-way through a highly predictable multi-token collocation or proper name (the piece just before an almost-forced continuation), e.g. "Hunting|ton Beach", "BNP Par|ibas", "all over| the| world", "where| you| are", "|real estate"; near-identical tokens (e.g. " the" in "around the world") also appear among the strongest suppressors, so it is best read as a weak, unstable collocation-continuation position signal rather than a content detector.

L11·N5894unmasked layer
This neuron has no single lexical trigger — it fires weakly and diffusely mid-sentence on continuation tokens inside formal/factual expository prose (e.g. the "Cross" of "Crossfire", "Week" before a number, plural "-s" in an org name, modal "should", infinitival "to"), while being suppressed on casual, conversational/first-person wording ("bubble wand", "you should try", "one special", "something else").

Fires on the word completing a self-referential discourse pointer — phrases where the writer refers to other parts of the text/instructions ("what I'm about to **say**", "I'll **explain** later", "as shown/link **below**", "a **recap**"); the mirror-image negative pole hits similar meta-discourse words ("the **following** procedure", "give **you** an example", "I'**ll** be honest").
